text: Plenty of systems log something, error messages, request timings. That's not the same as an audit trail, a record built specifically to answer who did what, to which data, when, and with what outcome.

A usable audit entry answers five questions every time. Who, the authenticated identity, not a shared account that could be anyone. What, the specific action and which record or field it touched. When, a precise, consistently-formatted timestamp. From where, the originating system or IP address. Outcome, whether the action succeeded, failed, or was denied. A log line that just says user accessed customer data is close to useless for an investigation.

A worked entry: timestamp, actor as a specific email and role, action READ, resource naming the exact customer ID and fields touched, source IP, outcome SUCCESS. Every field answers one of the five questions. If that customer later complains about their data being viewed without cause, this entry is exactly what an investigation pulls up first.

A log is itself a sensitive asset, it often contains the same personal data it's describing, and if an attacker can edit or delete entries after the fact, the audit trail stops being trustworthy evidence of anything. Tamper-evident or append-only storage, plus the same least-privilege principle applied to any other sensitive data, address this. And logs create a real tension with retention, you want them kept long enough to support an investigation, but they're personal data too, so most organizations set a distinct, usually shorter, retention period just for logs.
Long enough to be useful, short enough not to become its own breach liability. Next up: breach response concepts, what happens when all of this gets tested for real.
